## Statement

Sequential emulation exploits repeated eligibility: a new trial is emulated at each decision point, and a person eligible at many points contributes to many of them. The resulting within-person dependence has been addressed: clustering by person, and confidence-interval procedures for survival outcomes compared across the sandwich estimator, nonparametric bootstrap, jackknife and a linearized estimating function bootstrap, which covers better in the small-sample, low-event-rate regime that motivates the design. What has not been addressed is the calendar-time structure. Trials begun at different times occur under different treatment availability, guidelines and background risk, so a pooled estimate assumes an effect common to start times that differ in all three. Trial start is not conventionally modeled flexibly, treatment-by-start-time heterogeneity is not conventionally examined, and trial-specific estimates are not reported alongside the pooled one, so a pooled effect resting on incompatible starts is invisible.

## Why it is open

Testing the common-effect assumption costs the efficiency the design was adopted for, since trial-specific estimates are individually imprecise by construction. A person's later eligibility is itself a consequence of earlier untreated survival, so the trials are linked causally rather than only statistically, and whether that is innocuous depends on the outcome model being correct, which is the thing under test. Reporting per-start estimates also complicates a paper whose selling point was a single efficient number.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Caniglia EC, et al. Emulating target trials to avoid immortal time bias: an application to antibiotic initiation. Epidemiology 2023](https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000001601) | A worked sequential emulation showing how repeated decision points remove immortal time bias where treatment can begin at many times. |
| [Inference procedures in sequential trial emulation with survival outcomes: comparing confidence intervals based on the sandwich variance estimator, bootstrap and jackknife. Stat Methods Med Res 2025](https://doi.org/10.1177/09622802251356594) | Compares four variance procedures for sequential trial emulation and recommends the linearized estimating function bootstrap in the regime that motivates the design. |
| [Causal inference in survival analysis using longitudinal observational data: sequential trials and marginal structural models. Stat Med 2023](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.9718) | Sets out the sequential-trials estimator alongside marginal structural models for survival outcomes. |
| [Su L, et al. TrialEmulation: an R package to emulate target trials for causal analysis of observational time-to-event data. arXiv 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12083) | Implements the sequence expansion and censoring weights the design requires. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Model trial start flexibly rather than adjusting it away, examine treatment-by-start-time heterogeneity, and report trial-specific estimates alongside the pooled one, so a pooled effect resting on incompatible start times is visible. Cluster by person as standard, and use a person-level bootstrap where uncertainty from the estimated weights is material rather than assuming the sandwich estimator suffices. Establish whether the efficiency gain survives the correct variance treatment, since the case for the design has usually been made under the naive variance.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.

**The source said.** "Sequential emulation exploits repeated eligibility: a new trial is emulated at each decision point, and a person who is eligible at many points contributes to many trials. This uses the data better than a single baseline emulation and it introduces three complications together. The same person appears in many nested trials, so the observations are dependent in a way the pooled analysis must handle. Trials begun at different calendar times occur under different treatment availability, guidelines and background risk, so calendar time confounds the pooled contrast unless it is modeled. And a person's later eligibility is itself a consequence of earlier untreated survival, which links the trials causally rather than merely statistically. The efficiency gain is real and it is what makes these complications easy to overlook."

**What was wrong with it.** The variance half of the claim is answered. Confidence-interval procedures for sequential trial emulation with survival outcomes have been compared across the sandwich estimator, nonparametric bootstrap, jackknife and a linearized estimating function bootstrap, with the last recommended in the small-sample, low-event-rate regime that motivates the design. The entry asked for that work as though it had not been done. What survives is the calendar-time half and the reporting practice.

**Dissent.** literature dissented (overstated): The entry asks for variance estimators that account for repeated participation across nested trials and for a check of their coverage against a bootstrap over persons. That work has been done. A 2025 Statistical Methods in Medical Research paper compares confidence intervals for sequential trial emulation with survival outcomes across the sandwich variance estimator, nonparametric bootstrap, jackknife and a linearized estimating function bootstrap, and finds the last has better coverage in the small-sample, low-event-rate, low-treatment-prevalence regime that motivates the design. Sequential trials and marginal structural models were compared for survival outcomes in 2023. The dependence half of the entry is therefore substantially answered and should not be published as open. The calendar-time half, that pooling across start times assumes a common effect and that trial-specific estimates are not reported, is untouched by this work and survives. codex dissented (overstated): Repeated eligibility does create within-person dependence, but the pinned implementation already addresses the standard version of that problem: TrialEmulation clusters its sandwich covariance by the original person identifier. It also includes trial start period in the pooled outcome model by default and accepts user-specified trial-period formulas, including interactions for effect heterogeneity. Calendar time confounds a pooled person-trial contrast only when it predicts both treatment and outcome; treatment-effect variation across start times is a separate effect-modification issue. Likewise, only a pooled model constrained to one treatment coefficient assumes a common effect. Later eligibility changes the eligible survivor population, but this is part of the sequence of trial-specific protocols and does not make validity depend specifically on outcome-model correctness. The efficiency gain is also not guaranteed after accounting for correlation and variable weights. Remaining work concerns coverage when weights are estimated, finite-sample behavior, diagnostics for treatment-by-start-time heterogeneity, and clearly defined standardization across changing eligible populations. Those are legitimate methodological and reporting questions, but they do not support the asserted high-severity claim that basic variance and calendar-time methods are missing. grok dissented (supported-with-caveat): Inverted-prior search finds substantial 2024–2025 work on two of the three complications the entry bundles, so the problem is not open as a blank slate. On repeated participation and design-induced dependence, Limozin, Seaman and Su (arXiv 2407.08317; Stat Methods Med Res 2025) run a dedicated simulation comparing sandwich, nonparametric bootstrap, linearised estimating-function bootstrap and jackknife CIs for marginal risk differences under sequential trial emulation (STE), explicitly because the same patient can enter many nested trials. They report that sandwich/bootstrap/jackknife can account for that correlation, that sandwich is conservative when weight uncertainty is ignored, and that LEF bootstrap has the best small/moderate-sample coverage. That is exactly the variance and person-level bootstrap coverage work the agenda’s “direction” asks for; TrialEmulation is the implementation vehicle they use. On calendar-time confounding of pooled contrasts, DeMonte, Shook-Sa and Hudgens (arXiv 2403.18115) formalize nested trial emulation when the effect is allowed to vary over calendar time and/or time since treatment, provide a trial-effect-homogeneity test, and estimate trial-specific as well as calendar-time-varying vaccine effectiveness. That is the “model calendar time as effect modifier and report trial-specific estimates alongside the pooled one” program, at least in the vaccine setting where calendar-time heterogeneity is most obvious. Keogh et al. (Stat Med 2023) already recommended formal tests of trial-by-covariate interactions and compared sequential-trial efficiency to MSM-IPTW. What remains open, and why this is only partial: (1) Limozin evaluates CI coverage and computation, not a definitive redesign verdict that the efficiency case for STE survives person-clustered variance in general applications; sandwich conservatism means naive SEs can still overstate precision relative to person-level resampling. (2) DeMonte’s calendar-time-varying MSMs are developed and simulated for nested vaccine trials; they do not close the problem for arbitrary sustained pharmacoepidemiologic strategies or for routine non-VE sequential emulations that still pool under a common-effect assumption. (3) The third arm (later eligibility as a consequence of earlier untreated survival, so that trials are causally linked and the selection process depends on the outcome model being correct) is not resolved by either paper; no 2024–2026 work found identifies that selection away or shows it is innocuous under weak conditions. Package activity (TrialEmulation, SEQTaRget on CRAN) implements expansion and weighting but does not by itself close the identification/inference gaps. Cited prior work (Caniglia 2023; Su arXiv 2402.12083) illustrates and software-izes the design rather than solving the three complications. Queries that returned no full solution: “sequential trial emulation selection later eligibility untreated survival”; “efficiency gain sequential nested trial person-cluster sandwich vs naive”; general-journal 2024–2026 searches for a single paper closing all three arms together. Net: variance and calendar-time arms are partially methodologically addressed with evaluated tools; the bundled “still open and easy to overlook” framing is still useful but overstates residual openness if it ignores Limozin 2025 and DeMonte 2024.

glm
:   **open / supported.** The claim is internally consistent and proportionate. It identifies three genuine complications of sequential target trial emulation—design-induced dependence from repeated participation, calendar-time confounding across start times, and survival-conditioned later eligibility—and frames them as overlooked rather than impossible to address. The reasoning for openness is coherent: pooling requires a common-effect assumption that calendar-time variation challenges; the dependence has no natural clustering variable beyond the person; and the selection process depends on outcome-model correctness, which is the inferential target. None of these are asserted as structural impossibilities; they are framed as current-practice gaps, which is the correct register. The proposed directions (model calendar time as effect modifier, derive person-level variance estimators, compare efficiency under correct variance) are constructive and imply the problems are solvable, reinforcing that the claim is about practice rather than principle. The scope is appropriate: the claim does not say sequential emulation should be abandoned, only that its efficiency gain conceals complications that need methodological attention. The severity is proportionate to the cost of a wrong pooled estimate in a treatment-effect decision. I cannot verify whether specific software or recent papers already resolve all three complications together, so I do not downgrade from open, but the claim as stated does not depend on any software capability assertion.

Decision path
:   `R3:partially-solved(n=3/4) → R7:counter-and-support-both-present`
